1: Israel's descendants multiply. A new Pharaoh enslaves them and orders the midwives to kill the baby boys. The midwives fear God and refuse.
The midwives' courage shows that God's law comes before a ruler's command.
2: A Hebrew mother hides her baby in a basket on the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter finds and raises him. As a man, Moses kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew and flees to Midian.
God prepares a rescuer inside Pharaoh's own house. He hears his people's groaning.
3: God speaks to Moses from a bush that burns without being consumed. He sends him to bring Israel out of Egypt and reveals his name: "I AM WHO I AM."
God's name says that he simply is: the source of all being, always present.
4: Moses protests that he is no speaker. God gives him signs and appoints his brother Aaron to speak for him. Moses returns to Egypt, and the people believe.
God works through reluctant and limited people.
5: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go. He refuses and makes the slaves' work harder. The people blame Moses.
Things often get worse before God's rescue appears.
6: God tells Moses, "I am the Lord; I will free you, redeem you, and take you as my people." The people are too crushed to listen. A family record of Moses and Aaron follows.
God's promise does not depend on the people's mood.
7: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent and swallows those of Pharaoh's magicians. The Nile turns to blood. Pharaoh's heart stays hard.
The plagues show that the gods of Egypt are powerless.
8: Three more plagues strike Egypt. Even the magicians admit, "This is the finger of God." Pharaoh promises to release Israel, then goes back on his word.
Repentance made only under pressure does not last.
9: Disease kills Egypt's animals, boils break out, and hail destroys the crops, while the land where Israel lives is spared. Pharaoh says "I have sinned" and then changes his mind.
God distinguishes his people. Pharaoh's words without change are empty.
10: Locusts eat what the hail left, and thick darkness covers Egypt for three days. Pharaoh offers compromises; Moses refuses them all.
God does not bargain over his people's freedom to worship him.
11: Moses announces the last plague: every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's son to the slave's.
12: Each family kills a lamb without blemish, marks the doorposts with its blood, and eats it in haste. The Lord passes over the marked houses and strikes Egypt's firstborn. Israel leaves that night.
Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, whose blood saves from death. The Last Supper was a Passover meal.
13: Firstborn and the pillar of cloud
Every firstborn is to be consecrated to God, and the feast of unleavened bread kept each year. God leads the people by a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night.
Israel is to remember its rescue and teach it to its children.
14: Pharaoh's army traps Israel by the sea. Moses stretches out his hand, the waters part, and Israel walks through on dry ground. The sea closes over the Egyptians.
This is the great saving act of the Old Testament and a figure of baptism. It is read at every Easter Vigil.
15: Moses and Miriam lead the people in a song of victory. Three days later they grumble over bitter water, and God makes it sweet.
Praise turns to complaint very quickly. God is patient with them.
16: The hungry people long for Egypt. God sends quail and a daily bread from heaven called manna, enough for each day, with a double share before the Sabbath.
Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven. "Give us this day our daily bread" echoes the manna.
17: At God's word Moses strikes a rock and water flows. Amalek attacks, and Israel wins while Moses' arms are held up in prayer by Aaron and Hur.
Paul says the rock was Christ. Prayer wins the battle, and we need others to hold us up.
18: Moses' father-in-law sees him judging every case alone and advises him to appoint capable, honest men to share the load.
Good leaders delegate. Moses is humble enough to take advice.
19: God offers Israel a covenant: "You shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." The people agree. God comes down on the mountain in fire, thunder and smoke.
God rescued Israel first and gave the law afterwards. Obedience is a response to grace.
20: God speaks the ten words: worship him alone, honour his name and his day, honour parents, do not kill, commit adultery, steal, lie or covet.
The commandments are the basic terms of friendship with God and a summary of the natural moral law.
21: Rules protect servants and set fair penalties for violence and negligence. "An eye for an eye" limits punishment to match the harm done.
These laws restrain revenge. Jesus will go further and ask for mercy.
22: Thieves must repay. God forbids mistreating foreigners, widows and orphans, and charging interest to the poor.
God takes the side of those with no one to defend them.
23: Do not spread false reports or take bribes; help even your enemy's animal. Rest the land every seventh year, and keep three yearly feasts. God promises an angel to guard the way.
24: Moses reads the law aloud, the people promise to obey, and he sprinkles them with the blood of sacrifice. The elders see God and eat in his presence. Moses goes up the mountain for forty days.
Jesus echoes these words at the Last Supper: "This is my blood of the covenant."
25: God asks for offerings to build a sanctuary so that he may dwell among his people. He describes the ark of the covenant with its mercy seat, the table for the bread, and the golden lampstand.
God wants to live with his people. The Church sees the ark as a figure of Mary, who carried the Lord.
26: Instructions for the tent itself: curtains, frames, and a veil separating the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies.
That veil is torn when Jesus dies, opening the way to God.
27: Plans for the bronze altar of sacrifice and the court around the tent. A lamp is to burn there always.
The sanctuary lamp in Catholic churches continues this sign of God's presence.
28: Aaron and his sons are set apart as priests. The high priest wears a breastpiece with twelve stones bearing the names of the tribes.
The priest carries the people on his heart before God.
29: Aaron and his sons are washed, clothed, anointed and consecrated over seven days. A lamb is to be offered every morning and evening.
God promises, "I will dwell among the people of Israel and be their God."
30: Instructions for the altar of incense, a basin for the priests to wash, the anointing oil and the incense.
Incense is a sign of prayer rising to God and is still used in the liturgy.
31: God fills Bezalel with his Spirit and with skill for the work. The Sabbath is the sign of the covenant. God gives Moses two stone tablets.
Artistic skill is a gift of God's Spirit, to be used for his glory.
32: While Moses is on the mountain, the people have Aaron make a golden calf and worship it. Moses breaks the tablets and pleads with God not to destroy them.
Idolatry comes right after the covenant. Moses offers himself for his people, as Christ will.
33: Moses asks to see God's glory
God speaks with Moses "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend". Moses begs God to go with them and asks to see his glory. God lets his goodness pass by while shielding him.
Moses wants God himself, not only God's gifts.
34: God proclaims his name: "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love". New tablets are made. Moses comes down with his face shining.
This description of God as merciful is repeated all through the Bible.
35: The people bring gold, cloth, wood and skill, each as their heart moves them.
Generosity for God's house comes from willing hearts.
36: The craftsmen start building. The people give so much that Moses has to tell them to stop.
37: Bezalel makes the ark, the table, the lampstand and the altar of incense as God described.
Care in making holy things is itself an act of worship.
38: The altar of sacrifice, the basin and the courtyard are completed, and the materials used are counted.
The work is done with honesty and exact accounts.
39: The priestly garments are finished. Moses inspects everything and blesses the people, because they did it just as the Lord commanded.
Faithful obedience in details matters to God.
40: The tabernacle is set up on the first day of the year. The cloud covers it and the glory of the Lord fills it. The cloud guides Israel through all its journeys.
The book that began in slavery ends with God living in the midst of his people.
